summary: **Planning instructional dialogue on rights and restrictions**

item.text:
Nell pauses over the transfer schedule when you ask.

“How do I tell what the cinema owns from what’s on loan? And what restrictions do I need to check before I handle something?”

“Strictly, the trust owns the collection. It leases the building.” She turns the schedule towards you. “For material acquired with the old business, start here. Match the item or group to the signed transfer papers. Purchases should have an invoice or receipt; gifts should have a signed gift record. A loan has its own agreement and still belongs to the lender.”

She traces one entry with her finger: a group of programme files transferred to the trust in 2024.

“A note saying ‘Picture House’ isn’t proof. Neither is finding something on our shelves. If you can’t connect it to an acquisition record, don’t choose a likely answer. Record the ownership as unconfirmed, note exactly where you found it and bring it to me.”

Nell unlocks the loan cupboard again and takes out Bea’s shallow album box. She leaves the album inside while placing the signed agreement beside it.

“First, make sure the object matches the agreement. Then check the lender, the end date and the permitted activity. Some loans allow full cataloguing. Others might permit only a box-level inventory, supervised handling or a condition check without unfolding anything.”

She points to Bea’s terms.

“This one permits inventory and written condition descriptions until the thirtieth of October. That allows the handling needed to describe it. It does not allow scanning, publication or display. Those are separate permissions.”

The agreement has no requirement for gloves or supervised access, but Nell indicates the album’s binding through the open box.

“Paper and books: clean, dry hands, pencil at the table. If you find damp, mould, insects, loose photographs or a binding that’s failing, stop. Permission to handle something doesn’t mean we should keep handling it when its condition makes that unsafe.”

She closes the album box and returns it to the cupboard.

“Also, owning the physical item doesn’t necessarily give us copyright or permission to publish personal information. Those questions matter later, even for trust-owned material.”

After locking the cupboard, Nell returns its key to the permissions folder. On the blank catalogue record, she enters the transfer schedule’s reference under **PROVENANCE**, then marks the owner as the trust.

“That is the paper trail for the first file. We’ll describe what’s actually inside it next.”
